text: Book 22
The Killing of the Suitors – The Disloyal Maids Cleanse the Hall and Are Then Hanged
Odysseus threw off his old rags and leapt onto the wide floor with his bow and quiver full of arrows. He poured the arrows onto the floor at his feet and declared,
The great archery contest is over. Now, let's see if Apollo will grant me the power to hit another target—one that no man has ever struck before.

Odysseus immediately aimed a deadly arrow at Antinous. Antinous was just lifting a two-handled golden cup to drink his wine. The cup was already in his hands. He never saw death coming. Among all the feasting guests, who would imagine that one man, no matter how brave, would stand alone and kill him? The arrow struck Antinous in the throat, and the arrowhead went clean through his neck. He collapsed instantly, dropping the cup from his hand. A thick stream of blood gushed from his nostrils. He kicked the table away, sending everything on it crashing to the floor. Bread and roasted meats were scattered and soiled.

The suitors erupted in chaos when they saw one of their own struck by an arrow. They all sprang from their seats in dismay, looking frantically at the walls, but there were no shields or spears to be found. They glared at Odysseus, furious, and shouted,

Stranger, you'll pay dearly for shooting people like this! You won't live to see another contest. You're a dead man! The one you killed was the finest young man in Ithaca, and for this crime, vultures will feast on your body!

They spoke this way because they believed Odysseus had killed Antinous by accident. They had no idea that death was hanging over every single one of their heads. But Odysseus glared at them and spoke.

You dogs! Did you really think I wouldn't return from Troy? You've squandered my wealth, forced my female servants to your beds, and tried to marry my wife while I was still alive! You feared neither gods nor men. Now, you will die!
Odysseus's words turned them pale with terror. Every man frantically looked around, searching for a way to escape to safety. But only Eurymachus dared to speak.
If you are truly Lord Odysseus,
he began,

then your words are just. We have done great wrong in your lands and in your house. But Antinous, the ringleader of all our sins, already lies dead. Everything was his doing. He didn't truly want to marry Queen Penelope; he didn't care much for marriage at all. What he truly desired was something else entirely, and Zeus did not grant it to him. He wanted to kill your son and become the most powerful man in Ithaca. Now that he has met the death he deserved, please spare the lives of your people. We will make everything right and fully repay you for all we have eaten and drunk in your house. Each of us will pay a fine worth twenty oxen, and we will continue to offer you gold and bronze until your heart softens. Until we have done this, no one can complain about your anger towards us.
Odysseus glared at him again and said,

Even if you gave me everything you possess now, and everything you ever will possess, I will not stop my hand until I have made every single one of you pay in full. You must fight, or try to run for your lives. But I promise you, not a single one of you will escape!
Their hearts sank as they heard his words. But Eurymachus spoke up once more.

My friends, this man will show us no mercy! He'll stand right there and shoot us down until every one of us is dead. So, let's fight back! Draw your swords, and use the tables as shields against his arrows. Let's rush him fiercely, drive him from the floor and the doorway. Then we can get into town and raise such an alarm that his shooting will surely stop!

No sooner had he finished speaking than he drew his sharp, double-edged bronze sword and, with a loud cry, charged at Odysseus. But Odysseus, without a moment's hesitation, shot an arrow that struck him in the chest. The arrow pierced his nipple and buried itself deep in his liver. He dropped his sword and collapsed, doubled over his table. In his death throes, he struck the ground with his forehead, sending the cup and all the food crashing to the floor. He kicked at the stool with his feet until his eyes finally closed in darkness.

Just then, Amphinomus drew his sword and charged straight at Odysseus, trying to force him away from the doorway. But Telemachus was quicker. He struck Amphinomus from behind. The spear pierced him between the shoulders and went straight through his chest. Amphinomus fell heavily to the ground, striking the earth with his forehead. Telemachus quickly pulled back, leaving his spear in the body. He feared that if he paused to pull it out, one of the Achaeans might rush him, cutting him down with a sword or knocking him over. He ran straight back to his father's side and said,
Father, let me bring you a shield, two spears, and a bronze helmet for your head. I'll arm myself too, and bring armor for the swineherd and the cowherd. We all need to be armed!
Go quickly and get them!
Odysseus replied.
Do it before my arrows run out. If I'm left alone, they might manage to push me away from the door.

Telemachus did as his father commanded and hurried to the storeroom where the armor was kept. He chose four shields, eight spears, and four bronze helmets with horsehair plumes. He brought them to his father as fast as he could and armed himself first. The cowherd and the swineherd also put on their armor and took their places beside Odysseus. Meanwhile, as long as his arrows lasted, Odysseus shot the suitors one by one, and they fell, piling up on top of each other. When his arrows ran out, he propped his bow against the end wall of the house, next to the doorpost. He then slung a sturdy shield, made of four layers of hide, over his shoulders. On his noble head, he placed a finely crafted helmet with a horsehair crest that nodded menacingly. He gripped two formidable bronze-tipped spears tightly.

Meanwhile, there was a secret trapdoor in the wall, and at one end of the hall, an exit led to a narrow passage. This exit was sealed by a well-made door. Odysseus ordered Philoetius to guard this door, as only one person could attack it at a time. Then Agelaus shouted loudly,
Can't someone go through the trapdoor and tell the people what's happening? Help would come at once, and we could quickly put an end to this man and his deadly archery!
That won't work, Agelaus,
Melanthius replied.

The entrance to that narrow passage is dangerously close to the outer courtyard's entrance. Even one brave man could stop any number of people from getting in. But I know what I'll do. I'll bring you weapons from the storeroom. I'm certain Odysseus and his son have hidden their arms there!

With that, Melanthius, the goatherd, slipped through the back passages of Odysseus's house and headed to the storeroom. There, he chose twelve shields, along with twelve helmets and spears. He brought them back as quickly as possible and handed them over to the suitors. Odysseus's heart sank when he saw the suitors putting on their armor and brandishing their spears. He instantly realized the immense danger they were in. Odysseus turned to Telemachus and said,
Someone among the women inside is helping the suitors against us, or it could be Melanthius himself.
Telemachus replied,

Father, the fault is mine. It's entirely my fault. I left the storeroom door open, and they were sharper than I was. Eumaeus, go and close the door. Then check to see if it's one of the women, or if it's Melanthius, Dolios's son, as I suspect.
They were still talking when Melanthius headed back to the storeroom for more weapons. The swineherd Eumaeus saw him. He turned to Odysseus, who was beside him, and said,

Your Majesty Odysseus, brave son of Laertes, it's that villain Melanthius, just as we suspected! He's going to the storeroom. If I can overpower him, should I kill him? Or should I drag him here so you can take your own revenge for all the evil he's done in your house?
Odysseus replied,

Telemachus and I will hold these suitors in check, no matter what they do. Both of you, go back and bind Melanthius's hands and feet behind his back. Throw him into the storeroom and lock the door tightly. Then tie a rope around his body and hang him from a high pillar, close to the rafters. He will die slowly in agony.

They immediately did as Odysseus had commanded. They headed to the storeroom and entered before Melanthius even saw them. He was busy searching for weapons deep inside the room. So the two men stood on either side of the door and waited. A moment later, Melanthius came out. He held a helmet in one hand and an old, dry-rotted shield in the other. Laertes had used that shield when he was young, but it had been discarded long ago, and its straps had come undone. The two men pounced on him. They grabbed him by the hair and dragged him, struggling, to the ground. They bent his hands and feet tightly behind his back and bound them painfully, just as Odysseus had ordered. Then they tied a rope around his body and hoisted him up a high pillar, close to the rafters. The swineherd Eumaeus then shouted triumphantly at Melanthius,

Melanthius, you'll spend the night on a comfortable bed, just as you deserve! When morning comes from the streams of Oceanus, you'll know very well it's time for you to drive in the goats for the suitors' feast!

They left Melanthius in cruel bondage. Then, having put on their armor, they closed the door and returned to take their places beside Odysseus. The four warriors now stood in the cloister, fierce and full of fury. However, the suitors in the main hall were still brave and numerous. Just then, Athena, daughter of Zeus, approached them. She had taken on the voice and form of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her. He said,
Mentor, please help me. Don't forget your old comrade, who has done you many favors. Besides, aren't we age-mates?
But all the while, Odysseus was certain she was the goddess Athena. The suitors on the other side raised an uproar as soon as they saw her. Agelaus was the first to criticize her.
Mentor!
he shouted.

Don't let Odysseus trick you into siding with him and fighting us suitors! Here's what we'll do: once we've killed this father and son, we'll kill you too. You'll pay for it with your life. After we kill you, we'll confiscate all your property, both inside and outside your house, and combine it with Odysseus's wealth. Your sons and daughters won't live in your house, and your wife won't be able to live in the city of Ithaca!
This made the goddess Athena even more furious. She scolded Odysseus angrily.
Odysseus,
she said,

your strength and prowess are not what they were when you fought the Trojans for nine long years for noble Helen! Back then, you killed countless enemies, and Priam's city fell because of your cunning plans. So why have you so lamentably lost your courage now? You are here in your own home, on your own land, facing these suitors! Come on, my brave friend, stand by my side and watch how Mentor, son of Alcimus, fights your enemies and repays your kindness!

But the goddess Athena would not grant him full victory just yet. She wanted to test the prowess of Odysseus and his brave son even further. So, she flew up to one of the rafters in the cloister roof. She sat there, transformed into a swallow.

Meanwhile, on the suitors' side, Agelaus son of Damastor, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus son of Polyctor bore the brunt of the fight. Among all those still fighting for their lives, they were by far the most valiant. The others had already fallen under Odysseus's arrows. Agelaus shouted to them,

Friends, he'll soon have to stop fighting! Mentor has left, doing nothing but bragging. They are standing at the doors with no support. Don't all aim at him at once. Instead, six of you throw your spears first. See if you can win glory by killing him! Once he falls, we won't need to worry about the others!

They threw their spears as Agelaus commanded, but the goddess Athena made them all useless. One hit the doorpost. Another struck the door. The pointed shaft of yet another hit the wall. As soon as they had avoided all the suitors' spears, Odysseus said to his men,
Friends, I think we'd better throw our spears into their midst now! Otherwise, they'll finish all the harm they've done to us by killing us outright!

So they aimed straight ahead and threw their spears. Odysseus killed Demoptolemus. Telemachus killed Euryades. Eumaeus killed Elatus. The stockman Philoetius killed Pisander. All of them fell dead to the ground. As the other suitors retreated into a corner, Odysseus and his men rushed forward. They pulled their spears from the bodies of the dead and took them back into their hands.

The suitors threw their weapons once more, but the goddess Athena made most of their attacks miss. Some spears struck the cloister pillars. Others hit the door. Another sharp spear struck the wall. Still, Amphimedon managed to lightly graze the skin on Telemachus's wrist. And Ctesippus succeeded in scratching Eumaeus's shoulder above his shield. But that spear flew on and fell to the ground. Then Odysseus and his men fiercely charged into the crowd of suitors. Odysseus hit Eurydamas. Telemachus hit Amphimedon. Eumaeus hit Polybus. Next, the stockman hit Ctesippus in the chest and taunted him, saying,

Foul-mouthed son of Polytherses, don't be so foolish as to curse wickedly another time! Let your words follow heaven's will, for the gods are much stronger than men. I give you this advice as a gift. It repays you for kicking Odysseus when he was begging in his own house!

As the stockman spoke, Odysseus stabbed Damastor's son with a spear in close combat. Telemachus hit Leocritus, son of Evenor, in the belly. The spear pierced him completely. Leocritus fell forward, face-first, to the ground. Just then, the goddess Athena, from her seat on the rafter, raised her deadly Aegis shield. The suitors' hearts quailed in terror. They fled to the other end of the courtyard like a herd of cattle maddened by gadflies during the longest days of early summer. It was like eagle-beaked, hook-taloned vultures from the mountains swooping down on small birds. These birds cowered in flocks on the ground. They could neither fight nor fly, and onlookers enjoyed the sight. Odysseus and his men likewise fell upon the suitors, striking them down on all sides. Horrible groans erupted as their brains were crushed, and the ground was soaked with their blood.
Then Leodes caught Odysseus's knees and pleaded,

Lord Odysseus, please have mercy on me and spare my life! I never wronged any of the women in your household, either in word or deed. In fact, I tried to stop the others. I saw what they were doing, but they wouldn't listen to me. Now they are paying for their folly. I was their sacrificing priest. If you kill me, I will die without having done anything to deserve it. I will receive no thanks for all the good I tried to do.
Odysseus looked sternly at him and replied,

If you were their sacrificing priest, then you must have prayed many times that it would be a long time before I returned home. You must have prayed that you might marry my wife and have children by her. Therefore, you must die.

After saying this, Odysseus picked up the sword that Agelaus had dropped when he was killed. It was lying on the ground. He then struck Leodes on the back of his neck. Leodes was still speaking, but his head rolled in the dust.

The minstrel Phemius, son of Terpes, had been forced by the suitors to sing to them. Now he tried to save his life. He stood near a secret door, holding his lyre. He hesitated, wondering whether to flee out of the cloister and sit by the altar of Zeus in the outer courtyard. Both Laertes and Odysseus had offered many ox bones there. Or should he go straight to Odysseus and grasp his knees? In the end, he decided it was best to grasp Odysseus's knees. So he laid his lyre down between the mixing bowl and a silver-decorated chair. Then he approached Odysseus, grasped his knees, and said,

Lord Odysseus, please have mercy on me and spare my life! If you kill a minstrel like me, who can sing for both gods and men, you will regret it later. I compose all my own songs, and heaven grants me all kinds of inspiration. I could sing to you as if you were a god! So please, don't be so quick to cut off my head. Your own son, Telemachus, will testify for me. I did not want to frequent your house and sing for the suitors after their meals. But they were too many and too strong; they forced me.
Telemachus heard him and immediately went up to his father.
Stop!
he cried.

This man is guiltless. Don't harm him. And let's spare Medon too. He was always good to me when I was a boy. Of course, that's assuming Philoetius or Eumaeus hasn't already killed him. Or that he hasn't fallen in your path while you were raging through the courtyard.

Medon heard Telemachus's words. He had been crouching under a chair, hidden by covering himself with a freshly flayed heifer's hide. Medon threw off the hide. He approached Telemachus and grasped his knees.
Here I am, young master!
he said.
So please, stay your hand and speak to your father. Otherwise, he will kill me in his rage against the suitors. They wasted his wealth and were so foolishly disrespectful to you.
Odysseus smiled at him.

Don't be afraid. Telemachus has spared your life. From now on, you'll see, and you can tell others, how much better good deeds turn out than bad ones. So, you and the bard, go out to the outer courtyard, away from this slaughter, while I finish my work here.

The two men rushed out to the outer courtyard. They sat by the great altar of Zeus, trembling with fear and looking around, still expecting to be killed. Odysseus carefully searched the entire courtyard to see if anyone had managed to hide and was still alive. But he found only bodies, all lying in the dust and covered in blood. They were like fish that fishermen had pulled from the sea and thrown onto the beach, gasping for water until the hot sun finally killed them. That's how the suitors lay, all piled up against each other.
Odysseus turned to Telemachus.
Call Nurse Eurycleia. I have something to say to her.
Telemachus knocked on the door of the women's quarters.
Hurry out,
he called.
You, the elder in charge of all the women in the house. Come outside; my father wants to speak with you.

When Eurycleia heard this, she unlocked the door of the women's room and came out, following Telemachus. She found Odysseus standing among the corpses, covered in blood and grime like a lion that had just devoured an ox. His chest and cheeks were entirely bloody, making him a truly terrifying sight. Odysseus was stained with gore from head to toe. Seeing all the bodies and such a vast amount of blood, she realized a great deed had been done and was about to shout for joy. But Odysseus stopped her.
Nurse,
he said,

celebrate in silence. Control yourself and don't make a sound. It's wrong to gloat over the dead. Divine judgment and their own evil deeds brought these men to ruin. They disrespected everyone who came near them, rich or poor. They met a miserable end as punishment for their wickedness and foolishness. Now, tell me which of the women in the house behaved badly and which remained innocent.
I'll tell you the honest truth, my son,
Eurycleia answered.

There are fifty women in this house whom we teach to card wool and do all sorts of housework. Of these, twelve have behaved improperly and were disrespectful to me and Queen Penelope. They showed no disrespect to young master Telemachus, because he has only recently grown, and the Queen never allowed him to give orders to the female servants. But I should go upstairs and tell your wife everything that has happened, for some god must have put her to sleep.
Don't wake the Queen yet,
Odysseus replied.
Instead, tell the women who behaved badly to come to me.
Eurycleia left the hall to tell the women to come to Odysseus. Meanwhile, Odysseus called Telemachus, the shepherd, and the swineherd.
Begin,
Odysseus said,

to clear away the dead, and make the women help you. Then, get sponges and clean water to scrub down the tables and chairs. After you've thoroughly cleaned the entire hall, take those women into the space between the domed room and the outer courtyard wall. Then, stab them with your swords until they are completely dead, until they forget all their secret affairs with the suitors.

At this, the women came down together, weeping and wailing bitterly. First, they carried the dead bodies out and propped them up against each other in the gatehouse. Odysseus ordered them and made them work quickly, so they had to carry the bodies out. When they had finished this, they cleaned all the tables and chairs with sponges and water. Telemachus and the other two shoveled up the blood and grime from the floor, and the women carried it all away and put it outside. After they had made the whole place spotless and orderly, they took the women out. They trapped them in the narrow space between the wall of the domed room and the courtyard wall, so they couldn't escape. Telemachus said to the other two,
I won't let these women have an easy death. They were disrespectful to me and my mother, and they slept with the suitors.

With those words, he tied a sturdy ship's rope to one of the bearing-posts that supported the roof of the domed room. He strung the rope high around the building, ensuring that none of the women's feet could touch the ground. Just as thrushes or doves beat against a net set for them in a thicket as they return to their nest, meeting a terrible end, so too did the women, one by one, slip their heads into the nooses and die a most wretched death. Their feet twitched convulsively for a moment, but not for very long.

As for Melanthius, they dragged him through the hall into the inner courtyard. There, they cut off his nose and his ears. They pulled out his guts and threw them raw to the dogs, and then, in a rage, they hacked off his hands and his feet.
When they had finished this, they washed their hands and feet and went back into the house, for everything was now over. Odysseus said to his beloved old nurse, Eurycleia,

Bring me sulfur, which cleanses all impurities, and fetch fire also, so I may burn it and purify these halls. Go, moreover, and tell Penelope to come here with her ladies-in-waiting, and call all the other maidservants that are in the house.
Everything you've said is true,
Eurycleia answered,
but let me bring you some fresh clothes—a shirt and cloak. You shouldn't wear these tattered rags any longer. It's not proper.
First, light the fire,
replied Odysseus.

She brought the fire and sulfur, as he had asked her, and Odysseus thoroughly cleansed the halls, the inner courtyard, and the outer courtyard. Then she went inside to summon the women and tell them everything that had happened. The women came from their rooms with torches in hand and crowded around Odysseus to embrace him, kissing his head and shoulders, grasping his hands, and hugging him. He remembered each and every one of them, and felt a surge of emotion, as if he might burst into tears.
